en: A memory card smaller than your fingernail can now hold two terabytes.
How do they cram so much into something so tiny?
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
Let's open up the gadgets that store your stuff.
Every photo, video and game is really just ones and zeros.
A storage device has one job: keep them safe.
A hard drive has spinning platters and a tiny head on an arm.
It writes each bit by flipping tiny magnets to north or south.
To fit more, you add platters or shrink the magnets.
But make them too small and heat alone can flip them, wiping your data.
One trick is to overlap the tracks like roof shingles.
More fits, but rewriting files gets slow.
Solid state drives, USB sticks and SD cards use flash memory instead.
Each tiny cell traps electric charge, and it stays even when the power is off.
Early cells stored one bit, just two levels.
Now many store four bits, which means sixteen different levels in one cell.
But the cells sat side by side on a flat chip, like a town of tiny houses.
Shrink them more, and they start to disturb each other.
So engineers built up instead, like skyscrapers.
Today's chips stack cells in over three hundred layers, then pile several chips into one package.
So why is an SSD faster than a USB stick?
Its controller is a powerful brain that uses many lanes at once, like a giant highway.
A cheap stick gets just a narrow road.
Tiny magnets, trapped charges, and skyscrapers of cells.
That's how storage keeps growing.
Stay curious!
